title: My partner gives me the silent treatment to punish me
summary: The silent treatment as punishment: how to tell it from needing space, why apologizing keeps it going, and what to say instead.
body_markdown:
It's the second day. They answer direct questions with one word, or not at all. They talk to the dog, to their mom on the phone, to the person at the coffee counter, warmly, right in front of you. You've replayed the argument a dozen times looking for the moment you crossed a line. And part of you already knows how this ends: eventually you'll apologize, maybe for something you're not sure you did, they'll thaw, and nobody will ever mention it again.


If that's the pattern, you're not imagining the "punish" part. Not every silence is a weapon. But silence that switches on when you displease someone, holds until you give in, and switches off without a word is doing a job. It helps to see clearly what that job is.


## Needing space vs. making you pay


Lots of people go quiet in a fight because they're overwhelmed, and that's a different problem with different fixes (we cover it in[why some partners shut down during arguments](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-partner-shuts-down-during-arguments) ). The punishing kind looks different up close:


- **Space says when it's coming back.** "I need tonight, can we talk tomorrow?" Punishing silence has no end date, and the not-knowing is part of the point.
- **Space is about the conversation. Punishment is about you.** An overwhelmed partner avoids the topic. A punishing one withdraws everything: eye contact, affection, the goodnight, sometimes even acknowledging you're in the room.
- **Space ends in talking. Punishment ends in a thaw.** After a real break, you get back to the issue. After the silent treatment, they act as if nothing happened, and bringing it up risks round two.
- **Space isn't conditional.** The punishing version tends to end once you've apologized, conceded, or shown you're sorry enough.


One bad night doesn't make someone a punisher. Most people have sulked at some point. What matters is whether this is the go-to move every time you raise something they don't like.


## What it slowly does to the person on the other side


There's an arc we see in Maia conversations with people living with this. Early on, they describe the silence as the problem. Later, they describe something quieter: they've started editing themselves ahead of time. They skip the complaint, swallow the request, laugh off the comment that stung, because two days of cold isn't worth it. A lot of them say they've apologized for things they still don't think were wrong, just so the house would feel normal again. By that point the silent treatment barely has to happen. The threat of it does the work.


That's the real cost. Not the quiet itself, but how much of your own voice you've traded away to avoid it. If you recognize yourself here,[giving in just to end the argument](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/i-always-give-in-to-end-the-argument) probably feels familiar too.


## Why apologizing to end it keeps it going


This isn't a criticism of you. When someone you love goes cold, reaching for them is instinct. But look at the loop: the silence starts, you get anxious, you apologize or give ground, the warmth comes back. Every round proves it works. And the thing you originally raised quietly drops off the agenda, which may have been the point all along.


Chasing doesn't help much either. Following them from room to room, asking "are you still mad?", the long text at midnight. Each one hands over a little more of the control the silence was built to get.


## What to do instead


You can't make someone talk. You can stop the silence from working, and you can say plainly what's going on.


1. **Name it once, calmly, and leave the door open.** "I can tell you're upset. I'm here when you want to talk, and I'm not going to keep asking." Then actually stop asking.
2. **Don't apologize for what you didn't do.** If you got something wrong, own that specific part. Don't buy the peace back with an apology you don't mean.
3. **Keep living your life.** Make dinner, see your friend, go to bed at your usual time. Not as a counter-punishment. Just a refusal to put everything on hold until they decide you've suffered enough.
4. **Raise the pattern later, when things are warm.** Not during a silence, and not in the first hour after one. "When we disagree, you sometimes stop talking to me for a day or two. It feels like I'm being punished for bringing things up. I want us to be able to disagree and still talk. What would you need instead?"
5. **Offer a better exit.** Some people punish with silence because nobody ever showed them another way to be angry. Agreeing that either of you can say "I need a few hours, let's come back to this at eight" gives them a way out of the conversation that doesn't make you pay for it. That's a[healthy boundary](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/boundaries-the-secret-to-a-stronger-relationship) for both of you, not just a request.


**Instead of:** "Are you seriously still not talking to me? I already said I was sorry."


**Try:** "I'm going to stop asking. When you're ready, I'm here, and I still want to talk about what I brought up."


## When it's part of something bigger


If you've done all of this (named it gently, offered a real alternative, stopped rewarding it) and the silences still come every time you have a need, that tells you something. The issue isn't your technique anymore. It's whether your partner is willing to give up a tool that keeps working for them.


Sometimes the silent treatment is one piece of a larger pattern: silences that run a week or longer, being cut off from money, plans or people while it lasts, living in a constant state of[walking on eggshells](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/walking-on-eggshells-in-my-relationship) , anger or threats waiting on the other side of the quiet. Used that way, silence is emotional control, not a communication style. If that sounds like your relationship, talk to someone you trust, or call the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233 in the US). They help with emotional and controlling behavior too, not only physical abuse.


If you're in the middle of a silence right now, or trying to work out how to bring up the pattern without setting off another one, you can talk it through with Maia. Sometimes it just helps to get clear on what you actually want to say before you're standing in the kitchen trying to say it.
